name: Umar Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Umar, thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Kessler Auto Parts in Dunmere. We supply garages with brake pads, filters, batteries and the like, and I buy from about fifty suppliers. I come in at half seven, check what the garages ordered overnight, and see what we're short of. Then I match part numbers to car models, send orders, and chase late deliveries. Gerda, the senior buyer, signs off big orders, and I'm still the one learning the catalogue.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks. What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when a tricky part turns up and a garage can finish a car. What wears me out is the endless checking, one wrong digit and you've got the wrong brake disc on a pallet. I've used an AI assistant a few times to summarise catalogues, but I always double check. At home there's Lena, who works in a care home, and our two, Emil and Anja.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the hype was big and the reality's a handy tool. At work I'd keep using it for emails and catalogues, like now. If anyone asked me online, I'd say let's wait for the boring results before we panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm relieved, but I'm not comfortable. Kessler's margins are thin, and a competitor that sells parts online straight to garages can take a chunk anyway, AI or not. Our mortgage rate reset last spring and it costs about eighty a month more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Keep learning small things, like the AI summary for catalogues, so I'm not the slowest buyer. I'd ask Gerda to let me take on the brake and filter ranges, which are higher value. And I'd put two hundred a month in a separate account, which I haven't managed so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. A bit tense when the post comes, because the post is usually a bill. But I sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the competitor selling online. How much does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite a bit. If a garage can order from a website in two clicks at the same price, it doesn't need a salesman, and it doesn't need me to buy for the salesman. It's slow, but the real threat to my job is a website that lets a garage order in two clicks, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The mortgage reset, what happened there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our fixed rate ended and the new one added about eighty a month. That doesn't sound like much, but our savings are under a month. Lena picked up two extra shifts a month at the care home to cover it.

say: I'd say the hype was big and the reality is a **handy tool**.
I'd tell people to wait for the boring results before they **panic**.
think: I'm relieved but not **comfortable**; Kessler's margins are thin.
A competitor selling online to garages can take a **chunk** anyway.
Our mortgage rate reset last spring and costs about **eighty** a month more.
do: Keep using AI summaries of catalogues so I'm not the slowest **buyer**.
Ask Gerda (my senior buyer) to hand me the brake and filter **ranges**.
Save two hundred a month in a separate **account**.
feel: **Tense** when the post arrives, since it's usually a bill, but I sleep fine.
S0.quote: The real threat to my job is a website that lets a garage order in two clicks, not AI.
fieldNote: Sees the **online competitor**, not AI, as the real risk even when AI is a plateau.
Mortgage reset and under a month saved leave him **uneasy**; his partner's extra shifts cover the gap.
Measured and numbers-led, with **no one to blame**.

steps.text: Use AI summaries of parts catalogues to keep pace as a buyer
Ask Gerda for the brake and filter ranges to buy
Save two hundred a month in a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we should be honest about who it hits first. At work I'd tell Gerda and the manager, Mr Bauer, that I'm happy to take on more with the tools if the pay moves with it. Online I'd stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking part numbers against car models, which is a lot of my week, is the exact thing software does well. If cuts come, I could see two of the four buyers going. Gerda retires in a year or so, and they may just not replace her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly, an evening a week. I'd find a course the company pays for, or pay it myself. I'd ask Mr Bauer to let me test the new fitment checker, so I'm one of the people who knows it. I'd save an extra hundred, and keep an eye on the two other parts firms in Dunmere. And Lena and I would sit down and set a budget, for the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A steady kind of worry. Not sleepless, but there. I'd think about it on the drive in, and it would shape every decision at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the company only keeps two buyers, what makes you one of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, being cheaper and being willing. I'm junior, so I cost less than Gerda, and I'd use the tools. But if they want experience, I'm the one on the outside. I can't control that, so I just work on the part I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the plan with numbers. Here's what we cut, here's what I'm learning, here's the date I'd start sending applications. She's calm, she'd say okay, and then she'd tell her sister, who'd worry for both of us.

say: I'd say it's a big change and we should be honest about who it hits **first**.
I'd tell my managers I'll take on more with the tools if **pay** moves with it.
think: Checking part numbers against car models is a lot of my week, and software does it **well**.
Two of the four buyers could go, and Gerda (the senior buyer) may not be **replaced**.
do: Take an evening **course** in the tools, paid by the company if possible.
Ask Mr Bauer (the manager) to let me test the new fitment **checker**.
Save an extra hundred, set a **budget** with Lena, and watch for other parts firms hiring.
feel: A steady **worry** I'd carry on the drive to work and into every decision at home.
S1.quote: Checking part numbers against car models, which is a lot of my week, is the exact thing software does well.
fieldNote: Treats the threat as a **numbers** problem: cost, willingness, and what he can control.
Wants to be among those who know the new fitment checker, a **practical** bid to stay.
Would give his partner a dated **plan**, while knowing she'd worry privately.

steps.text: Take an evening course in AI tools, asking Kessler to pay
Volunteer to test the new fitment checker for Mr Bauer
Save an extra hundred a month and set a budget with Lena
Watch for openings at the two other parts firms in Dunmere

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too short for anyone, and that both the companies and the government should have a plan. I'd keep it civil at work. I wouldn't give the kids any big headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is gone by then. It's the checking and the buying, all of it. Lena's care work holds longer, because someone has to lift and talk to a person, but one wage and a mortgage with no savings is not a number that works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd ask the company straight out what the plan is and whether there's a retraining deal. Second, I'd cut spending hard, the phone plan, the car down to one. Third, I'd take a hands-on course, like electric vehicle servicing, since I know the parts and robots take longer to arrive there. I'd ask the garages I deal with if they'd take me on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but organised. My stomach would be in a knot, but I'd make lists. Lists are how I cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three extra years for hands-on work mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means a mechanic's job could carry us to about 2031 and a bit beyond. I know the parts catalogue better than most apprentices, but I'm forty-three and I'd start at apprentice pay. That's maybe half what I earn now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cost do you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second car, we only really need it for Lena's early shifts. And the kids' two after-school clubs, Emil's football and Anja's piano, unfortunately. I'd explain it as a pause, not a stop.

say: I'd say two years is too short, and companies and government need a **plan**.
I'd keep it civil at work and give the kids no big **headline**.
think: My job is gone by then, both the checking and the **buying**.
My partner's care work holds longer, but one wage and a mortgage with no **savings** doesn't work.
do: Ask the company straight out about its plan and any **retraining** deal.
Cut spending hard: the phone plan, and the **second car**.
Take a hands-on course in electric vehicle **servicing** and ask local garages to take me on.
feel: **Alarmed** but organised: a knot in my stomach, and lists to cope.
S2.quote: I know the parts catalogue better than most apprentices, but I'm forty-three and I'd start at apprentice pay.
fieldNote: Alarm comes with **organisation**; he copes with lists and asks the company directly.
Turns his parts knowledge into a **hands-on** pivot, accepting apprentice pay of about half.
Pauses the kids' clubs rather than **ending** them, framing it as temporary.

steps.text: Sell the second car and cut the phone plan
Start an electric vehicle servicing course at the local college
Ask the garages I buy for if they'd take me on
Ask management what retraining help Kessler will give

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair window and people should use it. I'd tell colleagues to learn the tools now while the company's paying. And I'd say employers should plan, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm okay for two or three years, and the question is what comes after. The kids would reach the expensive years just as this lands. If I get this right, we're fine. If not, it's a hard one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd start the electric vehicle servicing course part-time, in the evenings. I'd put away three hundred a month so there's a real cushion by the end of the five years. And I'd keep using the AI tools so I stay useful at Kessler as long as possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady worry, with a plan on top. It's much easier than the two-year one, because I can make a plan and the plan has dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with five years than with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course and not just start it. With two years I'd be doing it in a panic and taking whatever pay they offered. With five years I could do a proper apprenticeship and be a service technician by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Lena say about you changing fields?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says she'd rather I do something I like than something I'm scared to lose. Her care home is short of staff, so she'd get more hours if we needed. It's not a grand plan but it holds.

say: I'd say five years is a fair **window** and people should use it.
I'd tell colleagues to learn the tools while the company is **paying**.
I'd say employers should **plan**, not wait.
think: I think I'm okay for two or three years; the question is what comes **after**.
The kids reach the **expensive** years just as this lands.
do: Start the electric vehicle servicing **course** part-time in the evenings.
Put away three hundred a month toward a real **cushion**.
Keep using the AI tools to stay useful at Kessler as **long** as possible.
feel: **Steady** worry with a plan on top, which is far easier than two years.
S3.quote: With five years I could do a proper apprenticeship and be a service technician by 2030.
fieldNote: Time converts alarm into **dated** steps: course, savings, apprenticeship.
Plans a switch into **hands-on** servicing, using what he knows about parts.
Partner supports him choosing work he likes, and her care home could give her more **hours**.

steps.text: Start a part-time electric vehicle servicing course in the evenings
Put away three hundred a month toward a real cushion
Keep using the AI tools at Kessler to stay useful

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough that nobody has an excuse. I'd tell people to start slowly, one skill at a time. I wouldn't be dramatic about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fifty-three, with the kids at university or just done. Ten years is long, but my cushion is thin and each year it's just as thin. The mortgage might be nearly cleared, which is the thing that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay down the mortgage with any extra, first, not savings. Keep my job and learn the tools. After year two, take the servicing course slowly, just in case. And I'd teach Emil and Anja that you should have a skill with your hands and a skill with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, in the day. At night I'd run numbers in my head about the mortgage, university and the cushion. It's a long road, but a thin one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pay the mortgage down before saving. Why that order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A house with no mortgage is the best cushion I can think of. If the job goes, the bills drop a lot. Savings run out in months, but a paid house keeps the family in one place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the date moves closer, say to 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd flip the order, savings first and the course now. I'd keep an eye on the news, but only the dull stuff, like what Kessler's competitors do. When they cut buyers, I'd move.

say: I'd say ten years is long enough that nobody has an **excuse**.
I'd tell people to start slowly, **one skill** at a time.
think: I'd be fifty-three with the kids just done at **university**.
Ten years is long, but my cushion is thin and stays **thin** each year.
do: Put any extra money toward the **mortgage** first.
Keep my job and learn the **tools**, then start the servicing course after year two.
Teach my kids to have a skill with their **hands** and one with people.
feel: Fine by day; at night I **run numbers** on the mortgage, university and cushion.
S4.quote: A house with no mortgage is the best cushion I can think of.
fieldNote: Treats a **paid-off house** as the best cushion, an unusual ordering of priorities.
Would **flip** the plan to savings first if competitors begin cutting buyers.
Ten years lowers the temperature, but thin savings keep him in **low-level worry**.

steps.text: Put extra money toward the mortgage before building savings
Keep learning the AI tools at Kessler
Start the servicing course slowly after the second year
Teach Emil and Anja a skill with hands and one with people

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no doubt. I could handle most of the others with a plan, but two years doesn't give me time to build one, and we have almost no savings. What would help is a retraining deal from the company, and some income support while I'm learning a new trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I don't blame anyone, and I don't think it helps. I just want somebody to tell me the real timeline early, so I can do the sums.

headlineQuote: I just want somebody to tell me the real timeline early, so I can do the sums.
portrait: Umar is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at an auto parts distributor, with a care-worker partner, two kids and a mortgage.
He is a pragmatic centrist who blames no one and copes with **numbers** and lists.
He uses AI now and then, and sees an online competitor as the more **immediate** threat to his job.
With under a month saved, he is anxious in most worlds and **alarmed** if AGI arrives in 2028.
biggestWorry: The 2028 case, because two years is not enough time to **build a plan** with almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A company **retraining** deal, income support while he learns a hands-on trade, and early honesty about the timeline.
